blocks.prompt: The Glass That Lets the Colors Out
blocks.text: A prism is a wedge of clear glass. There is no paint in it. There is no color in it at all. But hold a prism in a beam of sunlight and a rainbow lands on the wall. Where did the colors come from? They came from the light. Sunlight looks white to us, but white light is really every color mixed together. When the light goes into the glass, it bends. Each color bends by a different amount. Red bends the least. Purple bends the most. So the colors slide apart, like runners spreading out on a track. That is all a rainbow is. It is light with the colors pulled apart.

blocks.prompt: Where the Rainbow Was Hiding
blocks.text: For a long time, people believed a prism painted the light. They thought the glass was dirty, or flawed, and that the flaw stained the sunlight on its way through. It was a fair guess. The glass has no color, and then suddenly there are six colors on the wall. Where else could they come from? A young man named Isaac Newton tested the idea in the 1660s. He darkened his room, let one thin beam of sun in through a hole in the shutter, and put a prism in its path. A band of color stretched across the far wall. Then he did the clever part. He cut a small hole in a board, let only the blue stripe through, and sent that blue light into a second prism. If the glass painted the light, the blue should have changed. It did not. Blue went in and blue came out. The prism was not adding anything. The colors were in the sunlight the whole time, folded up together, and the glass simply spread them apart.

blocks.prompt: Why Glass Bends a Rainbow Out of Nothing
blocks.text: Nothing in the universe moves faster than light in empty space, about 186,000 miles every second. But light does not always travel through emptiness. Push it into water, or into a block of glass, and it slows down. In ordinary glass it drops to roughly two thirds of its top speed. That slowdown is the whole secret of the prism. Picture a line of marchers stepping off pavement into deep sand at an angle. The marchers on one end hit the sand first and slow down while the others are still on hard ground, so the whole line pivots. Light does the same thing. When a beam meets the slanted face of a prism, one edge enters the glass before the other, and the beam bends. Scientists call that bending refraction. Here is the part that makes the rainbow. The colors inside white light do not all slow down by the same amount. Violet is slowed the most, so it bends the hardest. Red is slowed the least, so it barely turns. Between them sit orange, yellow, green and blue, each bending a little more than the last. By the time the beam leaves the far face of the prism, the colors have separated into a fan. This spreading is called dispersion, and it is why a wedge of colorless glass can throw a rainbow across a wall. No color is created. Nothing is added. The prism only reveals what sunlight was carrying all along.

blocks.prompt: The Experiment That Took the Color Out of Glass
blocks.text: Before Newton, the prism was a toy and a puzzle. Everyone agreed it produced colors. The argument was about where those colors came from. The accepted answer, inherited from Aristotle and defended for centuries, was that pure light was white and simple, and that color was a kind of damage. Light passing through glass got weakened or shadowed, and the weakening showed up as red at one edge and violet at the other. Under that theory the prism was the author of the color. In 1666, in a room in Cambridge, Isaac Newton set out to settle it. He closed the shutters, cut a small round hole in one, and let a single beam of sunlight cross the darkness. A prism in its path threw a long band of color onto the far wall. That much was old news. Then Newton asked a better question: if the glass makes the color, what happens if you make it do the job twice? He set a board with a narrow slit in front of the colored band and turned the prism until only the blue stripe slipped through the slit. That isolated blue beam went into a second prism. If glass manufactured color, this beam should have been altered again, split further, stained a new shade. It was not. It bent a little more, as blue always does, and stayed stubbornly blue. Newton called this his experimentum crucis, the crucial experiment, because it killed one theory outright. Glass adds nothing. Sunlight is not simple at all. It is a bundle of colors traveling together, each one refracted by its own fixed amount, and the prism is merely a comb that separates them. Newton then reversed the whole effect. He gathered the spread colors with a lens and passed them into a second prism placed upside down, and the fan folded back into a single white beam. The rainbow went in and plain sunlight came out. It is worth noticing what he did there. He did not simply observe more carefully than everyone else. He built a situation in which the old theory and the new theory had to predict different outcomes, and then he looked. That method, far more than the pretty colors, is what made the prism famous.

blocks.prompt: A Wedge of Glass and the End of a Two Thousand Year Old Idea
blocks.text: A prism is an unimpressive object. It is a wedge of glass with polished flat faces, no moving parts, no color of its own. It is also the instrument that dismantled one of the longest running ideas in European thought, and the reason we can tell what a star is made of without going there. Start with the physics. Light in a vacuum travels at about 186,000 miles per second, and nothing beats it. Inside glass it slows to roughly two thirds of that speed, because the light interacts with the electrons in the material as it passes. If a beam meets the surface at an angle, one side of the wave front enters the slower material before the other side does, and the beam pivots. That pivot is refraction. The crucial detail is that the slowdown is not identical for every color. Violet light, with its short wavelength, is held back slightly more than long wavelength red. The difference is small, a matter of a percent or two, but a prism has two slanted faces and the beam is bent at both, so the small difference is applied twice and widened. The colors leave the glass fanned into a spectrum. Physicists call this dispersion, and it is not decoration. It is a measurement. Now the history. From Aristotle onward, the standard view held that white light was pure and simple and that color was a modification of it, something added by darkness, thickness, or flaw. The prism, in that reading, dirtied the light. In 1666 Isaac Newton went at the question sideways. He darkened a room, admitted one beam through a hole in the shutter, and used a prism to cast a spectrum. Then he screened off everything but a single stripe and fed that lone beam into a second prism. The old theory predicted further change. The beam refused. Blue entered and blue emerged, bent a little further, altered in no other way. Newton named this the experimentum crucis, and then closed the trap from the other side: with a lens and an inverted prism he gathered the whole spectrum and pushed it back into a single beam of white light. Color was not damage. White was the mixture, and the colors were the ingredients. Two thousand years of authority fell to a piece of glass and a dark room. One human touch survives in the standard list of colors. Newton could see no clear boundary between blue and violet, but he wanted seven names, because seven matched the notes of the musical scale and the known planets, and he liked the correspondence. So indigo was inserted. Every child who recites red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet is reciting a seventeenth century aesthetic preference alongside the physics. The instrument outgrew the man. Because each element absorbs and emits light at its own precise wavelengths, spreading starlight through a prism or its modern descendant, a diffraction grating, produces a barcode of bright and dark lines. Read the barcode and you know the star's composition, temperature, and motion. Helium was found in the spectrum of the sun before anyone found it on Earth. The expansion of the universe was first read as a shift in those lines toward the red end. All of it rests on a plain fact Newton proved in a shuttered room: the light already contains the answer, and the glass only spreads it out where we can look at it.
